p.x:
Every morning, I take the metro to school. The station entrance is near my house. I tap my card and go to the platform.
The train is usually on time. In the morning, there are lots of people, so I often have to stand. I hold on to a pole. People sometimes push to get on, but it's not nice!
I listen for my stop. When I hear, "The next stop is Chatuchak," I get ready. I use Exit 2, and my school is just five minutes' walk away.

Bangkok has a large public transport system. The BTS Skytrain runs above the streets, while the MRT runs underground. Most passengers use a smart card, which they tap at the gate. When the money runs out, they top up the card at the counter. Tourists can also buy a single ticket from a ticket machine.
During rush hour, the trains are packed. Each carriage has priority seats for elderly people, disabled passengers and pregnant women, and it's polite to give up your seat if someone needs it more than you. On the escalator, hold the handrail and stand on one side. Listen carefully to each announcement, especially at an interchange where you need to change lines.
Not every station is fully accessible. Some have a lift and a ramp, but others only have stairs, which makes travel difficult for wheelchair users.
For the final part of a journey, many people take a motorcycle taxi. In Chiang Mai, people use red songthaews. Long-distance travellers can take a train from Bangkok to other parts of the country. You can buy a return ticket, and some people choose an express train or travel first class. A sleeper train to Chiang Mai is a fun experience: you go to bed in Bangkok and wake up in the mountains! On older buses, a conductor still collects the money.

Cities around the world are investing heavily in public transport, motivated by concerns about congestion, air pollution and climate change. Some have introduced car-free zones in their centres, while others have replaced diesel vehicles with electric buses. Across Asia, high-speed rail networks now link major cities, offering an alternative to short-haul flights.
Yet building a good system is expensive. New metro lines require huge amounts of public funding, and many governments subsidise fares to keep them affordable. Critics argue that subsidies are unfair to taxpayers who never use public transport, while supporters reply that everyone benefits from cleaner air and less traffic. Most cities also employ a ticket inspector on some routes to catch the fare dodger who travels without paying.
For many passengers, the key factors are frequency and reliability: if a train comes every three minutes, few people need to check a timetable. Another challenge is the so-called last mile, the distance between a station or bus terminal and a person's final destination. If this part of the journey is difficult, many people will continue to drive. Ride-hailing apps, shared bicycles and electric scooters are increasingly filling this gap.
Ultimately, experts agree that public transport succeeds only when it is faster, cheaper or more convenient than the car.
